description: Most people finger hang the way that feels strongest, and that way loads the pulleys at multiples of the safe position. Stop doing finger hangs wrong: here is the open-hand way that builds the same cables without spending the rings.

lines: If your thumb wants to lock over, that is the lesson.
beats.title: THE HONEST TEST

beats.text: COMPARE IT TO YOUR CRIMP TIME

scenes.narration: Back to the ledge. | Doorframe, stair edge, | thick branch. | But today | the rule changes: | OPEN HAND ONLY. | Fingers draped | over the edge, | thumb hanging free, | not allowed | to lock over | your fingers. | Take your weight | on slowly. | Feet up | when it feels honest. | Time the hold. | It will be shorter | than your crimp time. | Much shorter, | for most people. | That gap | is the subject | of this video. | Got your TIME? | Keep it. | At the end, | I explain the gap.

lines: Open-hand time is the only honest score.
beats.title: THE REAL LINE

scenes.label: OPEN-HAND FINGER HANG, PAIN-FREE
scenes.narration: The line, for the open hand only: twenty seconds is trained, forty is elite, and under ten means the base comes first. But today the number that matters is the gap. If your crimp time is double your open-hand time, half your famous finger strength is borrowed from your pulleys, at interest rates your joints will eventually collect. A small gap, twenty percent or so, is the signature of a climber whose strength actually lives in the cable. So this episode is not really about a new test. It is about retiring a way of hanging that feels powerful and bills the wrong tissue, and replacing it with the position that builds the same strength honestly. Hold your open-hand number and your gap. Now let me show you exactly what the crimp does inside the finger, because once you see it, you will not unsee it.
scenes.sub: under 10 or any pain: build the base first - over 40: elite pulleys

beats.text: THE CRIMP BENDS THE CABLE HARD

lines: Sharp bend at the ring = multiplied load.
beats.title: THE ANGLE TAX

beats.text: THE THUMB LOCK ADDS EVEN MORE

scenes.narration: Look inside the finger in both positions. In the open hand, the tendon runs down the finger in a gentle line, and the pulleys hold it against a mild bend. The load on each ring is close to the load in the cable. Now crimp: the middle joint bends sharply, the tip joint hyperextends, and the tendon is forced around a corner exactly at the A2 pulley. Physics is merciless here. The sharper the bend, the harder the cable presses into the ring that guides it, and climbers' research puts the crimp's pulley load at several times the open hand's for the same bodyweight. Then the thumb locks over the top and adds its force to the bill. This is why the crimp feels stronger: it is a more aggressive machine. It is also why it injures: the machine's extra output is paid by the smallest tissue in the system. You are not choosing between strong and weak positions. You are choosing which tissue pays. The open hand also tells the truth about readiness. If the position itself feels unstable or tender at light loads, the base is not built yet, and the base is built with bars and towels, not ledges.

lines: The cable gets the same work.
The rings get a survivable share.
beats.title: THE TRADE

beats.text: TRAIN THE CABLE, SPARE THE RING

scenes.narration: Here is the trade, stated plainly, because it is better than it sounds. In the open hand, the finger flexor tendon works at nearly the same tension as in the crimp for the same hang. The cable, the tissue you are actually trying to build, loses almost nothing. What changes is the surcharge: the pulleys hold a fraction of the load, the joints sit at friendlier angles, and the whole system can be trained twice a week for years without the injury tax. The open hand is not the easy version of the exercise. It is the sustainable version, the one whose numbers in five years will bury the crimp artist who spent those years cycling between breakthroughs and pulley rehab. Climbers at the highest level do the overwhelming majority of their hang training open-handed or in mild positions, and save the full crimp for the moments that decide climbs. Train like the people who need their fingers for a living. They are not being cautious. They are being professional.

beats.label: FEET HELP UNTIL THE CABLE EARNS IT

beats.text: NO PAIN IS A RULE, NOT A HOPE

scenes.narration: So here is the right way, as a checklist you can run every session. One: open hand, fingers draped, thumb parked and useless. Two: load smoothly, taking two full seconds to transfer weight, never dropping onto the fingers or jumping for the ledge. Three: feet are training wheels, not cheating. Keep toes on the ground and unload exactly enough that the hold is hard but calm, then lift more weight week by week. Four: shoulders engaged, body quiet, no swinging, because every swing is a load spike the rings must catch. Five: come off smoothly, before failure, every time; the last wild second of a max hang is where good pulleys go to die. And the rule above all rules: pain in a finger joint ends the session, and lingering finger pain means you stop hangs and see a professional if it persists. Run this checklist for a season and your open-hand number will do something beautiful: it will approach your old crimp number, at a fraction of the risk. Six: log everything. Position, time, edge, and how the fingers felt the next morning. The log is what turns caution into a system.
Now hang with me, the right way. Open hand, smooth load, ten seconds, feet ready underneath you. Calm fingers, quiet body, zero pain. Go.

beats.text: TWICE A WEEK. THAT IS THE DOSE

scenes.narration: Your week, wrong way versus right way, side by side. Wrong: crimping from day one, max hangs to failure, fingers trained whenever motivation strikes. Right: two sessions a week, open hand only, feet assisting until the cable earns full weight, three hangs of ten to twenty seconds, each finished two seconds before it gets ugly. Between sessions, the rings rebuild, and rebuilding is not a metaphor; it is the slow protein work that decides whether next month's hangs feel solid or sinister. Add load by lifting the feet more and choosing slightly smaller edges over months, not days. Keep a simple log: position, time, and any finger sensations the next morning. Morning finger stiffness that grows week over week is your cue to hold the dose steady, not push it. The patient version of this exercise produces monsters. The proud version produces stories about the season someone lost to a pulley. Choose which story you are collecting. In a season, the patient man's open-hand number quietly becomes the number the proud man is still rehabbing toward.

lines: Open hand is the professional's grip.
beats.title: YOUR VERDICT

scenes.narration: So, your open-hand number and your gap. Under ten seconds: the base comes first, a month of bar and towel work, then retest. Ten to twenty with a shrinking gap: the conversion is working, your strength is moving into the cable where it belongs. Over forty open-handed: your fingers are genuinely elite, built the way professionals build them, at a price your pulleys could afford. Whatever your numbers are, they are measurements of position and readiness, not a grade on you. Drop your open-hand seconds in the comments, just the number. Retest in thirty days, open hand, same ledge. Stop doing finger hangs wrong, and this exercise will pay you for years instead of billing you for one bad month.
Same ledge, open hand, thirty days from now: that is the retest. If this way of training makes sense to you, subscribe, because we test a new cable every episode. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Stop Doing finger hangs Wrong: Train Your finger pulleys Instead
